articles.title: Six science-backed ways to combat heatwave sleep deprivation - The Telegraph

articles.full_text:
The idea of chugging half a litre of freezing liquid on rising (I’d say “on waking”, but I haven’t slept) gives me a creeping sense of dread, which only intensifies when my stomach gargles an otherworldly noise at first sip.
The idea is that the shock of the cold water will stimulate my nervous system and release adrenaline, thereby making me feel more alert. “It will definitely drop your core body temperature,” Dr Garley says, which sounds quite tempting on a 30C day, though he adds “it’s unlikely to do much more than that”.
It does actually sharpen me up a little first thing, bringing me out of my groggy state, though the effects are very short-lived.
Verdict: 6/10
2. Get out in the light first thing
“Light is probably the best free medicine that we have,” says Heather Darwall-Smith, sleep therapist, psychotherapist and author of How to Be Awake. It is a zeitgeber (or “time giver”) – external cues that help to keep your circadian rhythm in check. It is also proven to boost mood and increase motivation, which sound particularly helpful in the face of a bad night’s sleep.
Darwall-Smith says that “if you can get up and get outside, sit and have a cup of coffee in the garden” in the first half hour of the morning, that will help to nudge your body towards sleep by the time night comes, and keep you on track throughout the day. Cortisol (the stress hormone) rises as the hours pass, so “spending 10 minutes outdoors writing down what you’ve got to do for the rest of the day puts the brakes on stress before it starts to rise, and you get that valuable light that you need.”
Getting some light – and air – soon after waking definitely helps me to feel peppier. I’m far more ready for the day. Why haven’t I been having my morning coffee in the garden all heatwave?
Verdict: 9/10
3. Eat a carb-free breakfast
Multiple studies have linked higher protein consumption first thing to sustained satiety and energy levels throughout the day, as well as better sleep, while fewer carbohydrates have been found to increase the time spent in slow-wave sleep (or deep sleep), and reduce rapid-eye-movement sleep (in which our brain activity, heart rate and blood pressure remain at similar levels to when we’re awake).
“In the morning, your blood sugar is rising anyway, so we [in the world of sleep therapy] tend to be much more protein-based for breakfast than carb-based, because carbs can spike that blood sugar,” says Darwall-Smith.
I go for eggs, cucumber and beetroot, which stops me from feeling sluggish and keeps me going until lunch without a sugar crash.
Verdict: 8/10
4. Do a quick indoor HIIT workout
A 20-minute HIIT workout – which alternates short bursts of high-intensity training with brief recovery periods – promises to increase cardiovascular fitness, enabling the body to use oxygen more efficiently, and thereby improving alertness. The adrenaline release we get after physical activity helps to sharpen the senses, too; there is also a marked effect on memory and concentration, with one meta-analysis finding that exercise can prevent cognitive impairment caused by sleep deprivation. Tiring yourself out physically should also lead to a better night’s rest, with another paper showing that exercise also improved sleep quality.
“The benefit to doing it is great,” Darwall-Smith says of exercise, and “doing it indoors when it’s hot [is] excellent” (as this reduces chances of the body overheating, compared to exercising outdoors). She advises cooling down via stretching afterwards.
I drag myself to my local gym, the last place I want to be at any time, let alone when the sun is blazing outdoors. Unfortunately, the studies are right: a short bout of exercise does make me feel better, no matter how tired I felt before I pulled my lycra on.
Verdict: 8/10
5. Take a yogic ‘nap’
Yoga nidra (yogic sleep) and what Darwall-Smith calls the “secular version”, Non-Sleep Deep Rest (NSDR) – which was popularised by Stanford neuroscientist and longevity bro Andrew Huberman – are a form of relaxation that uses visualisation techniques to bring you into a state of very light consciousness. “I use them all the time,” she says of the methods which put you into light sleep for 20 minutes, “which is where you get the restorative benefits.”
The yoga nidra video I choose on YouTube starts off like a schlocky attempt at ASMR, but I definitely feel more relaxed as the guidance goes on, and I am told to welcome ebbs and flows in breath, to sense every part of my body, from sternum to little toe. I’m not sure I ever enter the state of ultra-light consciousness desired, and I feel more relaxed than energised, but there are worse ways to spend 20 minutes and it feels like it’s gone a little way to make up the hours I lost overnight.
Verdict: 7/10
6. Add salt to your water
Popularised by influencers, adding salt or electrolytes to water after a wakeful night is something Darwall-Smith recommends, too. After all, the hotter it is, the more we sweat, and the more electrolytes are lost. The logic goes that, after a sleepless night, adding a little salt (less than a pinch; you shouldn’t be able to taste it) to drinking water can help replenish lost sodium and chlorides, electrolytes which banish brain fog and keep us feeling alert.
I generally don’t add salt to my food, so the idea of putting it in my water doesn’t massively appeal. I follow the instructions to add just a dash and though it may be helping my hydration in ways I don’t realise, as I don’t notice any decrease in my groggy sleep deprivation.
Verdict: 4/10
And three ways to improve a hot night...
1. Have a warm shower before bed
While many think a cold shower is the secret to cooling down, the experts don’t agree. “If you have a lukewarm shower or even a hot shower, that flushes your skin,” Garley explains. “Flushing is one of the main ways that the body actually loses temperature” – by vasodilation, or the widening of blood vessels near to the skin’s surface, assisting the natural cooling our body goes through as bedtime approaches, and setting us up for a good night’s rest.
This one is a quick, easy win: I definitely feel cooler, and ready for bed a few minutes after stepping out of the shower.
Verdict: 9/10
2. Try the 20-minute rule
If you struggle to nod off, the 20-minute rule – getting up after tossing and turning and doing an unrelated, low-stimulation activity – can help promote sleep. “If you stay in bed awake, it just reinforces to your mind that the bed is a place for waking,” Dr Garley explains. “So we do encourage people to get up to find a relaxing and distracting activity while they wait for sleepiness to come back.”
I try reading a book – gentle yoga or listening to a podcast are alternative options – though it does feel a little wrong to be getting back out of bed before I’d actually fallen asleep in it. It’s not a technique I love.
Verdict: 5/10
3. Sleep outside
Darwall-Smith says that current record-breaking temperatures have led her to a more novel approach of staying cool at night. “I don’t operate very well in the sun at all, and I’ve been sleeping outside,” she admits. “It’s cooler, because the upstairs of my house is way too hot. If you can, then go for it,” Darwall-Smith advises.
Given the loft is a long way to drag a mattress and that I saw a fox, bats and a cat in my garden within about 30 seconds last week, I’m not brave enough to try this just yet. Besides, I don’t fancy being devoured by midges. The idea makes sense, though what happens to the underside of the mattress remains a mystery…
Verdict: No thanks
